body.text: North Korean support for Russia’s war against Ukraine has not materialized in the way Kyiv had originally predicted this past summer.

In August, Ukrainian intelligence assessed that the Kremlin had requested upwards of 30,000 more troops to support an autumn offensive. Kyiv also announced that Vladimir Putin and Kim Jong Un would meet sometime in September. It is now November, but no Russia-North Korea summit has taken place, and while there have been reports of additional North Korean troop deployments to Russia, there is no indication that tens of thousands more combat troops have moved from the Korean Peninsula to the front lines in Eastern Europe.

So, what happened, and where does North Korea’s involvement in the war stand today? Answering these questions requires revisiting the successive phases of North Korean support to understand how its role has evolved and where it might be headed.
Recapping North Korea’s Wartime Support

The Russia-North Korea relationship has a checkered past. Although the two countries’ trajectories have been intertwined since the end of World War II, their relationship has not always been cooperative. Thus, when the Kremlin launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the level of North Korean support that has emerged over the past four-and-a-half years was not a given.

In fact, North Korea’s response to Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014 was one of quiet diplomatic backing. Pyongyang avoided publicized statements of support, but still accepted the Kremlin’s territorial ambitions. Russian media reported that North Korea’s ambassador to Moscow conveyed his government’s backing on March 15, 2014. The following week, North Korea voted against United Nations General Assembly Resolution 68/262, which affirmed Ukraine’s territorial integrity and rejected the legitimacy of Russia’s annexation. Since then, North Korea has published atlases displaying Crimea as part of Russian territory.

At the outset of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Pyongyang’s response appeared to follow the same pattern of diplomatic support. In March 2022, North Korea was one of only five countries to vote against U.N. General Assembly Resolution ES-11/1, which condemned Russia’s invasion. It subsequently aligned its voting with Moscow on a series of related resolutions. In July 2022, Pyongyang recognized the independence of the Russian-backed “People’s Republic of Donetsk” and the “People’s Republic of Lugansk,” and expressed support for Russia’s annexation of the occupied Ukrainian territories that October.

North Korean support, however, took an important turn in the autumn of 2022. Russian forces were running short of munitions, leaving their positions vulnerable as Ukraine mounted a series of successful counteroffensives. This created an opportunity for North Korea to contribute to the war beyond diplomatic backing. Pyongyang’s extensive stockpiles of Soviet-era munitions offered Moscow a solution to its ammunition shortages.

In November 2022, the U.S. National Security Council released the first concrete intelligence indicating that North Korea was supplying military materiel to Russia. This marked the first instance during the war in which Pyongyang’s increased support played an indispensable role in extending the conflict. By providing critical munitions, North Korea enabled Russian forces to blunt the Ukrainian counteroffensive that had up to that point been proving successful.

Materiel support continued throughout 2023 as the Kim regime took steps to deepen its relationship with the Kremlin. The September 2023 summit between Putin and Kim at the Vostochny Cosmodrome accelerated these efforts, eventually setting the stage for the signing of their Treaty on Comprehensive Strategic Partnership during Putin’s reciprocal visit to Pyongyang in June 2024.
The formalization of their revitalized alliance arrangements provided the foundation for the next major evolution of North Korean support: direct military involvement in the campaign to retake Kursk.

In August 2024, Ukrainian forces crossed the Russian border into Kursk Oblast, advancing toward Sudzha and Korenovo. By October, the Ukrainian government had publicly disclosed intelligence that Russia was preparing to employ North Korean military personnel. Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate, part of the Ministry of Defense, assessed that North Korea was preparing to send as many as 12,000 personnel to Russia’s Kursk region. The U.S. Department of Defense subsequently confirmed that at least 10,000 North Korean soldiers were present to participate in the campaign.

This marked the second instance in which the escalation of North Korean support helped the Kremlin extend its war effort. By helping Russia expel Ukrainian forces from Kursk, Pyongyang enabled the Kremlin to eliminate an important bargaining chip for Kyiv in ceasefire negotiations. Ukrainian control of Russian territory could have provided leverage in negotiations over reciprocal withdrawals, where the tradeoff would have been Russian forces leaving occupied parts of the Donbas region in exchange for Ukrainian withdrawal from Kursk.

Following the expulsion of Ukrainian forces, North Korea continued providing materiel, labor, and other forms of assistance, with both Pyongyang and Moscow lauding the strength of their alliance. The question, however, was what might come next as the Kremlin sought to consolidate its gains and push Ukrainian forces completely out of their remaining footholds in the Donbas region.
Where Things Stand Today

Heading into autumn 2026, Kyiv assessed that the Kremlin had once again requested a surge of North Korean soldiers to support a forthcoming offensive. However, troop deployments of that magnitude have not occurred, and neither the Kremlin nor Pyongyang has given clear indications of their current or future designs for North Korean participation in Russia’s war effort.
There are four potential explanations here.

First, Ukraine’s assessment may have been based on faulty intelligence. The indications and warnings suggesting that the Kremlin was seeking so many additional North Korean forces may have been inaccurate or exaggerated, potentially reflecting shortcomings in human intelligence sources.

Second, Kyiv may have assessed the most dangerous course of action as the most likely one. In other words, there may have been more indicators suggesting that Pyongyang would not surge forces, but Ukraine focused on the comparatively fewer signs pointing to a major new deployment. Whether deliberate or unintentional, such an assessment was more likely to draw attention to the potential scale of North Korean involvement and the risks it posed.

Third, the Kremlin may have withdrawn its request. Putin could have reconsidered the merits of a major autumn offensive, whether because of political calculations involving the White House and the U.S. midterm elections or because Russia lacked the capacity to mobilize enough domestic forces to make a North Korean surge consequential on the battlefield.

Finally, Pyongyang may have declined the Kremlin’s request. While the Kim regime was comfortable overtly deploying troops in support of Russia’s campaign to retake Kursk within Russia’s prewar borders, it has not committed North Korean combat forces en masse to the front lines in occupied Ukrainian territories. This may represent a political red line, meaning that if the Kremlin asked for North Korean soldiers to participate in forward operations aimed at capturing the remainder of Donetsk, Pyongyang may simply have refused.

Rather than a mass deployment of troops, Ukraine has reported other forms of North Korean military involvement. These include the positioning of a North Korean missile unit in the Voronezh region of Russia and the deployment of 8,500 support troops, including drone operators, engineers, and deminers, to other rear areas. Meanwhile, Pyongyang has continued expanding its munitions production capacity while showcasing new drones, missiles, and other weapon systems that could eventually find their way to the battlefield.
Where Things Could Go
North Korea appears to have entered its endgame strategy for supporting Russia’s war effort.

The Kim regime well understands that full-scale hostilities will cease at some point, meaning that the Kremlin’s dependencies on North Korean troops and materiel will sharply decrease at some point. This in turn will affect the power dynamics between Pyongyang and Moscow. While the two countries have taken steps to insulate their bilateral relationship against the strategic shock of the war’s eventual termination, the Kim regime will have looked further afield as part of its five-year security and foreign policy designs produced during the Ninth Party Congress this past February.

As part of this endgame strategy, Pyongyang appears to be pursuing a status quo approach to its support for Russia while simultaneously extending outreach to its other major ally, China. The June 2026 summit between Xi Jinping and Kim Jong Un marked a renewed effort to strengthen bilateral ties, a trend that will likely continue as the Russia-Ukraine war eventually draws down.

Until then, North Korean support will remain a vital component of the Kremlin’s war effort. The material sustainment alone represents a substantial contribution, while troop augmentation, technical assistance, and labor provide critical backfills for Russian forces as they continue their campaign to drive Ukraine further beyond the current battle lines.

As winter approaches, another large deployment of North Korean combat troops to the front lines appears unlikely, though that possibility may warrant renewed attention during the spring thaw. In the meantime, Pyongyang’s current approach enables it to maximize the strategic benefits of its relationship with Moscow while minimizing its exposure to the outcomes of the war’s inevitable termination.
